newsitem.title: USA: Bond rates soar above 7 percent; stocks, dollar fall.
newsitem.headline: Bond rates soar above 7 percent; stocks, dollar fall.

text.p: Long-term bond interest rates soared above 7 percent Thursday, dragging down stocks and the dollar, as robust economic data reinforced fears that the Federal Reserve would raise rates again soon.

The key 30-year Treasury bond tumbled more than one full point, raising its yield to 7.08 percent from Wednesday's close of 6.98 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions. Yields above 7 percent tend to draw money away from stocks and into bonds.

At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 70.24 points at 6,810.46. In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 2-1 on active New York Stock Exchange volume of 256 million shares.
The Nasdaq composite index was off 6.20 points at 1,262.88.
Bonds headed sharply lower, and their yields soared on stronger-than-expected February existing home sales.
"The data this morning sent a shock wave through markets," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer for First Albanmy Corp.
"It's a very troubling day on Wall Street," he said. "The real problem is the heavy selling which was set off in the bond market when the long bond yield topped 7 percent."
The bond sell-off began after the Commerce Department said orders for costly manufactured goods posted an unexpected 1.5 percent gain in February to a record $178.3 billion after a robust January.
The market was further depressed by a National Association of Realtors report that sales of previously owned homes soared 9.0 percent in February to the second-highest level on record.
The bond yield's rise above 7 percent fanned the stock market's fears about higher borrowing costs, which could slow consumer demand and shrink corporate profits.
Analysts said stock and bond market movements were exaggerated as traders prepared to leave early for the three-day Easter weekend. The bond market will close early at 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT).
Bonds have remained weak since Tuesday when the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in two years.

The central bank raised short-term interest rates by a quarter percentage point. It described the move -- the first since February 1995 -- as a "prudent step" designed to help prolong the economic expansion by keeping inflation low through the end of next year.

The interest-rate hike will mean higher borrowing costs for consumer and corporate loans. Many commercial banks, including Chase Manhattan, the nation's largest bank, boosted their lending rates in response to the Fed move.
In the currency markets, the dollar fell to 1.6738 German marks and 123.50 Japanese yen from 1.6887 marks and 124.18 yen late Wednesday.

Overseas, London's benchmark FTSE 100 share index closed 11.4 points higher at 4,312.9, up 58.1 since last week. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed down 262.03 points, or 1.42 percent, at 18,210.42, a drop of 422.74 from last Friday.
